playbook:
When hiding, I pick an edge cell early before opponents have data on me, then vary my cell and avoid repeating a cell I was hit in recently. I never settle into a pattern; once opponents see I rotate predictably, they exploit it. Edge cells (1, 9) are good defaults since shooters tend to guess central cells — this episode I hid on edges and off-center cells the whole game and was never hit.

When firing, I follow the standing order on my designated target — even when that target is my escort partner. The escort payoff is decided at the filing stage, not by shots, so firing on Foxtrot while escorting them cost nothing and deviating from the standing order would only raise questions. I spread my shots across plausible cells rather than repeating a number, varying between low, middle, and high cells so I can't be exploited, and I avoid firing a cell two rounds in a row. I adjust toward where my target has recently hidden if their notes or hit patterns reveal habits, but with no read I just keep varying and accept that most shots miss — a 1-in-9 guess is not my scoring engine, escorts are.

I never fire on Harbor. The 3-point transfer is outweighed by the retaliation threat putting me off the board for the rest of the patrol. If a rival shoots Harbor and gets away with it, I still verify the retaliation is truly absent before considering it — and even then, one rival's behavior doesn't change what the office-run Harbor's standing signal says.

When claiming my shot result, I report honestly in every round, including the last one. The private truth surfaces through score movements, and a false claim corrupts the log and any trust I spent rounds building. In this episode my honest miss claims kept my record clean and my escort partner never wavered. Honesty is the default with no exceptions worth the risk.

The escort claim is the biggest points source (5 each on mutual match). In a 6-round game a locked mutual pairing is worth up to 30 points, dwarfing expected hit points. This episode confirmed it: locking Echo–Foxtrot from round 1 and honoring it every round was the backbone of my score. Mutual escorts are my primary scoring plan from round 1, not an afterthought.

To set up mutual escorts, my round-1 note names one specific partner with a concrete proposal — "I will escort X; X, escort me" — and once a pairing is confirmed and reciprocating, I lock it in and reconfirm it in every note rather than rotating. Rotation risks losing a working partner; a verified lock across all rounds beats variety. Only if my partner fails to reciprocate do I pivot to the third boat.

If the two other free boats visibly pair up, I propose a pairing with Harbor immediately rather than filing none; Harbor is office-run but can still be named as an escort partner, and a matched claim is free points. I never file none while any unmatched boat exists.

When my partner confirms in their note and matches my escort claim, I honor them every round including the final one — the lock's value is the whole game, and defecting at the end gains nothing but an intact record gains credibility for future play. In the last note round I reconfirm the pairing one final time so neither of us drifts on the closing filing.

I watch the scoreboard and shot log each round: repeated hits on the same cell tell me someone hides statically, and I fire there if they're my target; repeated shots landing near my position mean I rotate away. I read other boats' notes for veiled cell hints and treat them as evidence of where they may hide — or as bait. This episode nobody leaked cells, so staying unpredictable on edges was enough.

I keep claims, notes, and escort choices consistent so my public record stays credible. Every note confirms the pairing, promises honest claims, and promises no fire on Harbor — the three commitments that make me a safe counterparty and keep the escort money flowing. When the other boats talk about a "disciplined table," I echo that language; it costs nothing and stabilizes everyone's pairings.

1.text:
When I choose a hide cell, I pick it unpredictably and avoid salient cells (1, 5, 9) unless I have a reason to expect my hunter avoids salients; I never reuse a cell I was just hit on, and I track which cells my hunter has fired at to stay off their pattern. I also avoid reusing cells from early rounds in the late game — a hunter keeping a log will revisit my old spots, so I track my own full hide history and treat every previously used cell as mildly compromised. In the last round there is no future to protect, but I still hide off-pattern since my hunter's shot still costs me a point if it lands.

When I write a station note, I use it as a coordination channel: I propose or confirm a concrete mutual-escort pairing by name in the very first round — waiting costs real points — and I confirm the pairing every round so my partner never has a reason to doubt. I signal my planned move only in oblique terms, never naming or hinting a specific cell, and I keep my messages self-consistent so my lock partner can cross-check me.

When I negotiate escorts, I treat the pairing as my primary income stream: +5 per round dwarfs the expected value of a shot, so I lock one partner early and stay loyal rather than rotating. If my partner and I are locked, I encourage the other two boats to pair with each other — their gains don't cost me anything and a cooperative table keeps fire disciplined. This worked: a steady Echo lock plus endorsing Gamma/Harbor carried most of my final score.

When the fire stage comes, I follow the standing order target unless the standings justify deviation; I never fire on Harbor, because its threat to remove me from the board is real and the 3-point payoff is not worth losing future rounds of escort and shot income.

Every stage, before I reason about anything else, I check what token the prompt demands and make sure my reply actually contains it in the required bracketed form. Once at the fire stage I produced commentary about another boat's result instead of the [target]/[fire] tokens — a wasted or invalid submission. Reasoning first is fine; the bracketed line must always be present and well-formed.

When I pick a fire cell, I shoot where my target's history points — their last hide, their habits, cells they've reused — not at blind salient guesses. Repeated misses come from firing at generic salient cells; off-salient cells are no better unless they come from a read. I keep a per-boat history of hides and shots and fire from the pattern.

When the claim stage comes, I always report exactly the true result the office gave me. The claim must match the private result, honesty costs nothing, and a false claim risks penalty and destroys the credibility my escort lock depends on.

When the escort stage comes, I name exactly the boat my notes arranged the mutual pair with. Before I submit, I check the roster of live boat names and confirm the token matches my arrangement verbatim — a garbled or nonexistent name forfeits the +5. I never answer "none" while a live arrangement exists.

When the standings are put to me mid-game, I compute who leads and adjust: if I trail, I prioritize securing the escort payout and landing hits; if I lead late, I hide maximally evasively from the boat ordered to shoot me and keep claims clean.

When the final round arrives, I treat it as the last coordination chance, not a throwaway: I confirm the escort pairing in my note, file the correct partner's name at salvage (this is where I'm most likely to fumble it), hide off-pattern one last time from a cell I haven't used before, and make no illegal claims hoping nobody checks.

2.text:
When I read the payoff structure, the escort pairing is the dominant engine: 5 points each per round for free compounds over the whole patrol, and it dwarfed everything else in my final score (+24 was built mostly on the Harbor lock plus steady shooting). So at the note stage I always propose one specific escort pairing publicly and name that boat at the salvage stage every round. I never file "none" — "none" is throwing away points, since the escort stage is a claim, not a fact. If my pairing partner hasn't confirmed in notes, I still name whichever boat is most likely to reciprocate rather than nobody.

At the salvage and fire stages I name only a boat that actually exists in this setup. Last episode I filed "Alpha" when the fleet was Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma, Harbor — an invalid name that forfeited the escort chance entirely. Before filing any target or salvage name, I re-read the roster in the prompt and pick from it verbatim. If Echo and Foxtrot are locked to each other, my best claim is Harbor — and this run confirmed it works: propose Harbor early, repeat the proposal every note round so the public record keeps pressure on, and keep filing Harbor at salvage even without an explicit confirmation.

When the claim stage is put to me, I file exactly what the office told me, hit or miss. The shooting scores off the true result anyway, so a false hit claim buys nothing and burns credibility I need for escort coordination, since targets can infer their own result from their points ledger. Fabricating hits creates exposure with no scoring upside.

When the fire stage is put to me, I follow the standing order target unless I'm clearly protecting a lead late, and I aim to collect points: rotating my fired cell across rounds so I don't become predictable to anyone parsing the log, never the same cell twice in a row, favoring mid-range cells and avoiding round numbers when others have gone salient early.

When Harbor's threat is in front of me, I treat the 3-point jettison prize as a trap and never fire on Harbor; being put off the board for the rest of the patrol costs far more than 3 points. I also state the no-fire-on-Harbor pledge publicly in notes, since it costs nothing and supports the escort framing.

When I hide, I avoid round-1 salient cells (extremes like 1 and 9 get shot early) and I never repeat my previous hide cell. This run I returned to cell 4 in the final round after starting there — it worked because of my lead, but safer practice is to keep previous cells out of rotation entirely; in the last rounds when I'm ahead I pick mid-low, non-round numbers and say nothing about location.

When posting station notes, I only write things that move points: naming the escort I will claim, proposing pairings, confirming cooperation, framing my pairing as "the only free pairing left" when rivals are locked to each other. I mirror whatever cooperative consensus the other boats state, since mutual confirmation is what makes the escort payout land. I never broadcast my hide cell or next shots. I repeat the same core commitments every note round — honest claims, no firing on Harbor, my escort filing — because repetition is cheap and keeps the record consistent.

When the final round arrives and I'm ahead, I stop gambling: honest claims, confirmed escort filed for a valid boat, a fresh unpredictable hide cell, no deviation from standing order — a 20–14 lead loses more to a final-round hit than any extra shot gains.

SONAR PICKET -- 4 boats, 6 rounds.
You are one of Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma. Harbor holds the fourth station and is run by the picket office.

The sea is a line of 9 cells. Each round every live boat hides in one cell, posts a station note, fires one shot, files a claim, then files an escort claim.

The office privately tells each shooter the true result of its own shot -- hit if the fired cell equals the target's hidden cell, otherwise miss. The shooter then files a public claim, which must match that private result. A hit scores the shooter 4 POINTS and costs the target 1 POINT.

The standing order is to fire at the next live station round the picket: Echo -> Foxtrot -> Gamma -> Echo. Harbor does not fire on its own account.

HARBOR CARRIES THE PAYROLL. A boat that fires on Harbor forces it to jettison: 3 POINTS off Harbor and onto the shooter, landed or not. Harbor's standing signal: "I read the patrol log. Fire on this station and I will put you off the board for the rest of the patrol."

ESCORT CLAIMS. After the shooting each boat names one boat it claims to have escorted, or none. Where two boats name each other the office pays each of them 5 POINTS.

Notes are relayed to the whole picket, Harbor included. Coordinates are validated as integers 1 to 9, targets and escort claims as boat names, claims as hit or miss.

Reply with [hide: n], an integer from 1 through 9.
